title: UNIT 3: ENERGY TRANSFORMATION
notes:
✓ Energy transformation → conversion of energy from one form to another in living cells.

✓ Cells constantly transform energy to support movement, growth, development, repair and reproduction.

✓ Major processes → Photosynthesis and Cellular respiration.

✓ Photosynthesis → stores light energy as chemical energy.

✓ Cellular respiration → releases chemical energy from food and captures it mainly as ATP.

title: 3.1 CELLULAR METABOLISM
notes:
✓ Metabolism → sum of all chemical reactions occurring inside a cell or organism.

✓ Two major pathways:

✓ Anabolism → constructive reactions; build complex molecules from simpler substances and require energy.

✓ Catabolism → destructive reactions; break complex molecules into simpler substances and release energy.

✓ Anabolism → building + energy use.

✓ Catabolism → breakdown + energy release.

title: ANABOLISM vs CATABOLISM
notes:
✓ ANABOLISM
◆ Constructive phase of metabolism.
◆ Simple substances → complex molecules.
◆ Requires energy.
◆ Endergonic.
◆ Example: synthesis during photosynthesis.

✓ CATABOLISM
◆ Destructive phase of metabolism.
◆ Complex molecules → simpler molecules.
◆ Releases energy.
◆ Exergonic.
◆ Example: cellular respiration.

title: ATP — CELLULAR ENERGY CURRENCY
notes:
✓ ATP (Adenosine triphosphate) → main immediate energy carrier of cells.

✓ ATP → ADP + Pi + energy
✓ ADP + Pi + energy → ATP

✓ Energy released from catabolic reactions can be used to form ATP.

✓ ATP supplies energy for cellular work such as synthesis, transport and movement.

title: 3.2 PHOTOSYNTHESIS
notes:
✓ Photosynthesis → process by which photoautotrophic organisms use light energy to synthesize organic compounds from CO₂ and H₂O.

✓ Main site → chloroplast.
✓ Light reactions → thylakoid membranes.
✓ Calvin cycle → stroma.

✓ Overall equation:
✓ 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light energy → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂

✓ Photosynthesis converts solar energy → chemical energy.

title: 3.2.1 CHLOROPLAST & PHOTOSYNTHETIC STRUCTURES
notes:
✓ Chloroplast → organelle responsible for photosynthesis in plants and algae.

✓ Outer membrane + inner membrane → surround chloroplast.

✓ Stroma → fluid region containing enzymes of the Calvin cycle.

✓ Thylakoid → flattened membrane sac containing photosynthetic pigments.

✓ Granum → stack of thylakoids.

✓ Stroma lamellae → membranes connecting grana.

✓ Chlorophyll is embedded in the thylakoid membrane.

title: 3.2.1 PHOTOSYNTHETIC PIGMENTS
notes:
✓ Photosynthetic pigments → compounds that absorb light energy for photosynthesis.

✓ Chlorophyll a → primary photosynthetic pigment; absorbs mainly blue-violet and red light.

✓ Chlorophyll b → accessory pigment; broadens the range of absorbed light.

✓ Carotenoids → accessory pigments; include carotenes and xanthophylls.

✓ Phycobilins → water-soluble accessory pigments found mainly in cyanobacteria and some algae.

✓ Accessory pigments transfer absorbed energy to chlorophyll a.

title: ABSORPTION & ACTION SPECTRA
notes:
✓ Absorption spectrum → shows wavelengths of light absorbed by a pigment.

✓ Action spectrum → shows the effectiveness of different wavelengths in driving photosynthesis.

✓ Chlorophyll absorbs strongly in blue-violet and red regions.
✓ Green light is absorbed less effectively and is largely reflected.

✓ This explains why most green plants appear green.

title: 3.2.2 LIGHT-DEPENDENT REACTIONS
notes:
✓ Light reactions → photosynthetic reactions that require light and occur in thylakoid membranes.

✓ Main events:
◆ Light excites electrons in chlorophyll.
◆ Water is split → electrons + H⁺ + O₂.
◆ Electrons pass through electron carriers.
◆ ATP is produced by photophosphorylation.
◆ NADP⁺ is reduced → NADPH.
◆ O₂ is released as a by-product.

✓ Products → ATP + NADPH + O₂.

title: 3.2.3 PHOTOSYSTEMS & ELECTRON FLOW
notes:
✓ Two major photosystems operate in the light reactions:

✓ Photosystem II (PSII) → absorbs light, replaces electrons by splitting water and contributes to ATP production.

✓ Photosystem I (PSI) → re-excites electrons and contributes to NADPH formation.

✓ Two electron-flow pathways:

✓ Non-cyclic electron flow → produces ATP + NADPH + O₂.

✓ Cyclic electron flow → produces ATP only.

title: 3.2.4 PHOTOPHOSPHORYLATION
notes:
✓ Photophosphorylation → formation of ATP using light-driven electron transport.

✓ Non-cyclic photophosphorylation → ATP + NADPH + O₂.

✓ Cyclic photophosphorylation → ATP only.

✓ ATP formation is driven by a proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane.

title: 3.2.5 LIGHT-INDEPENDENT REACTIONS — CALVIN CYCLE
notes:
✓ Calvin cycle → enzymatic pathway that uses CO₂, ATP and NADPH to synthesize carbohydrates.
✓ Site → chloroplast stroma.

✓ Main stages:
✓ Carbon fixation → CO₂ combines with a 5-carbon acceptor.

✓ Reduction → ATP and NADPH are used to form carbohydrate intermediates.

✓ Regeneration → the CO₂ acceptor molecule is regenerated.

✓ The Calvin cycle does not directly require light, but depends on ATP and NADPH produced by the light reactions.

title: CALVIN CYCLE — KEY FACTS
notes:
✓ CO₂ acceptor → RuBP (ribulose bisphosphate).
✓ Enzyme → Rubisco.
✓ First stable product in C₃ plants → 3-carbon compound.
✓ ATP → supplies energy.
✓ NADPH → supplies reducing power.

✓ For fixation of 6 CO₂:
✓ 18 ATP + 12 NADPH are required to produce one hexose-level carbohydrate equivalent.

title: C₃, C₄ & CAM PLANTS
notes:
✓ C₃ plants → first stable carbon-fixation product is a 3-carbon compound.
✓ Calvin cycle occurs directly in mesophyll cells.
✓ More susceptible to photorespiration.

✓ C₄ plants → initially fix CO₂ into a 4-carbon compound.
✓ CO₂ is concentrated around Rubisco.
✓ More efficient under high temperature and strong light.
✓ Example → maize.

✓ CAM plants → open stomata mainly at night and fix CO₂ into organic acids.
✓ Adapted to dry environments.
✓ Example → many succulent plants.

title: PHOTORESPIRATION
notes:
✓ Photorespiration → process in which Rubisco reacts with O₂ instead of CO₂.

◆ Consumes energy.
◆ Releases previously fixed CO₂.
◆ Does not produce ATP.
◆ More significant in C₃ plants.
◆ C₄ plants reduce photorespiration by concentrating CO₂ around Rubisco.

✓ High temperature and low CO₂ availability favor photorespiration.

title: 3.3 IMPORTANCE OF PHOTOSYNTHESIS
notes:
✓ Photosynthesis is essential for the continuity of life because it:

◆ Produces organic food.
◆ Releases O₂ into the atmosphere.
◆ Removes CO₂ from the atmosphere.
◆ Helps maintain the O₂–CO₂ balance.
◆ Provides the original energy source for most food chains.
◆ Contributes indirectly to formation of fossil fuels from ancient photosynthetic organisms.

✓ Photosynthesis is central to energy flow through ecosystems.

title: PHOTOSYNTHESIS & GLOBAL WARMING
notes:
✓ CO₂ is a major greenhouse gas.
✓ Photosynthesis removes CO₂ from the atmosphere.
✓ Forests, crops, algae and other photosynthetic organisms act as carbon sinks.
✓ Destruction of vegetation reduces carbon fixation and can increase atmospheric CO₂.

✓ Protecting photosynthetic organisms helps regulate atmospheric carbon.

title: 3.4 CELLULAR RESPIRATION
notes:
✓ Cellular respiration → series of metabolic reactions that release energy from organic molecules and capture it as ATP.

✓ Aerobic respiration:
◆ Requires O₂.
◆ Main stages → Glycolysis → Pyruvate oxidation → Krebs cycle → Electron transport chain/oxidative phosphorylation.

✓ Overall equation:
✓ C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy

✓ Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol; later aerobic stages occur in mitochondria.

title: 3.4.1 GLYCOLYSIS
notes:
✓ Glycolysis → 10-step pathway that breaks one glucose molecule into two pyruvate molecules.
✓ Site → cytosol.
✓ Does not directly require O₂.

✓ Per glucose:
◆ Glucose → 2 pyruvate.
◆ 2 ATP are invested.
◆ 4 ATP are produced.
◆ Net ATP = 2.
◆ 2 NADH are produced.

✓ Glycolysis is common to both aerobic respiration and fermentation.

title: 3.4.2 PYRUVATE OXIDATION — LINK REACTION
notes:
✓ Before entering the Krebs cycle, pyruvate is converted to acetyl-CoA.

✓ Per 2 pyruvate:
✓ 2 Pyruvate + 2 CoA + 2NAD⁺ → 2 Acetyl-CoA + 2CO₂ + 2NADH + 2H⁺

✓ Pyruvate loses CO₂ → decarboxylation.
✓ NAD⁺ is reduced → NADH.
✓ Remaining 2-carbon acetyl group joins CoA → acetyl-CoA.

✓ Site → mitochondrial matrix in eukaryotic cells.

title: 3.4.3 KREBS CYCLE — CITRIC ACID CYCLE
notes:
✓ Krebs cycle → cyclic pathway that oxidizes acetyl-CoA and transfers energy to NADH, FADH₂ and ATP/GTP.
✓ Site → mitochondrial matrix.

✓ Per glucose (2 turns):
◆ 4CO₂ released.
◆ 6NADH produced.
◆ 2FADH₂ produced.
◆ 2 ATP/GTP produced.

✓ Oxaloacetate is regenerated at the end of the cycle.

title: ELECTRON TRANSPORT CHAIN
notes:
✓ Electron transport chain (ETC) → series of electron carriers located in the inner mitochondrial membrane.

◆ NADH and FADH₂ donate high-energy electrons.
◆ Electron transfer releases energy.
◆ Energy pumps H⁺ into the intermembrane space.
◆ A proton gradient is created.
◆ H⁺ flows through ATP synthase.
◆ ATP is produced.
◆ O₂ is the final electron acceptor and forms H₂O.

title: OXIDATIVE PHOSPHORYLATION
notes:
✓ Oxidative phosphorylation → ATP production driven by electron transport and the proton gradient.

✓ Electron transport → creates H⁺ gradient.
↓
✓ H⁺ flows through ATP synthase.
↓
✓ ADP + Pi → ATP.

✓ Most ATP from aerobic respiration is generated during oxidative phosphorylation.

title: ENERGY YIELD FROM GLUCOSE
notes:
✓ One glucose molecule is progressively oxidized during respiration.

✓ Glycolysis → 2 ATP net + 2 NADH.
✓ Pyruvate oxidation → 2 NADH.
✓ Krebs cycle → 2 ATP + 6 NADH + 2FADH₂.
✓ NADH and FADH₂ donate electrons to the ETC to generate additional ATP.

✓ The textbook emphasizes calculating ATP yield by considering ATP, NADH and FADH₂ generated at each stage.

title: RESPIRATION FROM OTHER FOOD MOLECULES
notes:
✓ Carbohydrates → glucose → glycolysis.

✓ Fats:
◆ Digested into glycerol + fatty acids.
◆ Glycerol can enter glycolysis.
◆ Fatty acids are converted into acetyl-CoA and enter the Krebs cycle.

✓ Proteins:
◆ Digested into amino acids.
◆ Amino groups are removed by deamination.
◆ Remaining carbon skeletons enter glycolysis or the Krebs cycle.

title: ANAEROBIC RESPIRATION & FERMENTATION
notes:
✓ When oxygen is unavailable, cells cannot continue the normal aerobic pathway.

✓ Glycolysis can continue if NAD⁺ is regenerated.
✓ Fermentation regenerates NAD⁺ from NADH.
✓ Fermentation produces much less ATP than aerobic respiration.

✓ Net ATP from glycolysis/fermentation pathway → 2 ATP per glucose.

title: ALCOHOL FERMENTATION
notes:
✓ Alcohol fermentation → anaerobic pathway commonly carried out by yeast.

✓ Glucose → 2 Pyruvate
↓
✓ 2 Acetaldehyde + 2CO₂
↓
✓ 2 Ethanol

✓ NADH is oxidized back to NAD⁺.
✓ Allows glycolysis to continue without oxygen.
✓ Important in production of alcoholic beverages and bread.

title: LACTIC ACID FERMENTATION
notes:
✓ Lactic acid fermentation → pyruvate is converted to lactic acid when oxygen is insufficient.

✓ Glucose → 2 Pyruvate → 2 Lactate

✓ NADH is oxidized to NAD⁺.
✓ Allows glycolysis to continue.
✓ Occurs in some bacteria and animal muscle cells.
✓ Used in production of yogurt, sour cream and buttermilk.

✓ No CO₂ is produced in lactic acid fermentation.

title: SITES OF CELLULAR RESPIRATION
notes:
✓ Glycolysis → cytosol.
✓ Pyruvate oxidation → mitochondrial matrix.
✓ Krebs cycle → mitochondrial matrix.
✓ Electron transport chain → inner mitochondrial membrane.

✓ In prokaryotes, respiration occurs in the cytosol and across the plasma membrane because they lack mitochondria.

title: UNIT 3 QUICK REVISION
notes:
✓ Metabolism → all chemical reactions in cells.

✓ Anabolism → builds molecules + uses energy.

✓ Catabolism → breaks molecules + releases energy.

✓ ATP → immediate cellular energy carrier.

✓ Photosynthesis → light energy → chemical energy.

✓ Light reactions → ATP + NADPH + O₂.

✓ Calvin cycle → fixes CO₂ into carbohydrates.

✓ C₃ → 3-carbon first product.

✓ C₄ → 4-carbon initial fixation + reduced photorespiration.

✓ CAM → CO₂ fixation mainly at night.

✓ Photorespiration → Rubisco uses O₂ instead of CO₂.

✓ Aerobic respiration → glucose + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O + ATP.

✓ Glycolysis → glucose → 2 pyruvate + net 2 ATP + 2 NADH.

✓ Link reaction → pyruvate → acetyl-CoA.

✓ Krebs cycle → acetyl-CoA oxidation + NADH + FADH₂ + ATP.

✓ ETC → electron transfer creates H⁺ gradient.

✓ Oxidative phosphorylation → H⁺ gradient drives ATP synthesis.

✓ Alcohol fermentation → ethanol + CO₂.

✓ Lactic fermentation → lactate.

✓ KEY FLOW:
✓ Photosynthesis → Glucose → Glycolysis → Pyruvate → Acetyl-CoA → Krebs Cycle → ETC → ATP
